title: Overview
excerpt: PerfectEvents is a white-label event ticketing platform: a public website where people discover and buy tickets, an Admin panel, an Organizer panel, and a pair
text: PerfectEvents is a white-label event ticketing platform: a public website where people discover and buy tickets, an Admin panel, an Organizer panel, and a pair of Flutter mobile apps (a customer app for browsing/buying/holding tickets, and a scanner app for door check-in). It's built to be resold and rebranded — one purchase, one deployment, your brand. How the product is put together The Laravel application (script/) is the whole backend: the public website, the Admin panel, the Organizer panel, and the /api/v1 that the mobile apps talk to. It ships as one install on one server. The mobile apps (flutter/) are optional. Selling entirely through the website works fine without ever touching Flutter. The apps exist for buyers who want a native customer app and/or door-staff scanner app in the app stores under their own name. Where to start If you're installing for the first time: Server requirements, then the installation wizard. If you only want to change how things look/behave without touching code, read Admin vs. rebuild first — it'll save you time. How this documentation is organized SectionWhat's in it Getting StartedThis page, server requirements, what you actually received, and the line between "change it in Admin" and "needs a code change." InstallationThe install wizard, hosting-specific notes (cPanel/VPS/subdirectory), and what to do when the installer complains. ConfigurationEnvironment variables, cron & queue workers, file storage/S3, caching, HTTPS. IntegrationsPayment gateways, email, SMS, social login, Firebase/push — one page per integration with the exact keys it needs. OperationsRunning the platform day-to-day: the Admin and Organizer panels, approvals, refunds, payouts, coupons, CMS, notifications, localization, backups. Mobile AppsBuilding, rebranding, and publishing the customer and scanner apps. MaintenanceUpdating the product without losing your customizations. ReferenceAPI overview, full settings reference, permissions matrix, troubleshooting index, FAQ. Conventions used in these docs Admin marks something you configure from a panel, no code involved. Rebuild marks something that requires editing source and rebuilding (mobile app icons, for example). Code you type goes in monospace; full commands are in code blocks.

title: Server Requirements
excerpt: PerfectEvents runs on any host that can run a modern Laravel application: shared hosting with cPanel, a VPS, or a container platform. There's nothing exotic in
text: PerfectEvents runs on any host that can run a modern Laravel application: shared hosting with cPanel, a VPS, or a container platform. There's nothing exotic in the requirements — no headless browser, no Node.js at runtime, no separate search service. Server software RequirementVersion PHP8.3 or newer MySQL8.0 or newer (MariaDB is not supported — the schema uses MySQL 8–specific JSON functions and generated columns) Web serverApache with mod_rewrite (shared hosting) or Nginx DiskA few hundred MB for the app itself, plus room for uploaded media (event covers, organizer logos) — budget for growth same as any media-heavy site Required PHP extensions Standard for any current Laravel app, plus two the platform specifically needs: BCMath, Ctype, cURL, DOM, Fileinfo, Filter, Hash, Mbstring, OpenSSL, PCRE, PDO + pdo_mysql, Session, Tokenizer, XML GD or Imagick — required for event/organizer image thumbnails (cover, card, and social-share sizes are generated automatically on upload) intl — used for currency and date formatting across locales The install wizard checks all of these automatically on its first screen and tells you exactly what's missing before you can continue — see the wizard walkthrough. File permissions The web server user needs write access to storage/ and bootstrap/cache/ — identical to any Laravel app. On shared hosting this is usually already correct for anything under your account; the installer's requirement checker will flag it if not. Background processing Two things need to run outside the request/response cycle: a cron entry (one line, every host supports this — including shared hosting) and a queue worker (ticket PDF generation, emails, image conversions, and push notifications are all queued so checkout stays fast). See Cron & queue workers for exact setup on shared hosting vs. a VPS with Supervisor. Outbound HTTP The server needs to make outbound HTTPS requests to whichever payment gateways, SMTP/SMS provider, and (if used) Firebase project you configure — most shared hosts allow this by default, but a locked-down VPS/firewall may need an explicit allow rule.

title: Admin vs. Rebuild
excerpt: Every setting in this product falls into one of two buckets. Knowing which bucket something is in before you start saves you from either editing code unnecessar
text: Every setting in this product falls into one of two buckets. Knowing which bucket something is in before you start saves you from either editing code unnecessarily, or hunting for a setting that was never going to exist as a toggle. AdminRebuild Where it livesAdmin → Settings, saved to the database, takes effect immediatelySource code / Flutter config files, needs a redeploy or app rebuild Who can change itAny super-admin, anytime, no developer neededWhoever manages your codebase ExamplesSite name, logo, brand color, currencies, languages, payment gateway keys, commission rate, coupon rules, notification templates, CMS pages, homepage layout blocksMobile app icon/splash/package id, adding a new payment gateway, changing the checkout flow itself, custom report types Why the split is where it is The rule of thumb: if it's a value (text, a color, a key, a limit, which gateways are on), it's a setting. If it's behavior (a new step in checkout, a new kind of ticket rule, a new integration this product doesn't already support), it's code. The web side (site name/logo/colors/currencies/languages) is fully Admin-driven — see Admin tour and the full settings reference. The one place this gets more involved: mobile apps The Flutter apps pull brand color, name, and logo from the server at runtime — same as the website. But an app's icon, splash screen, package id, and store listing are baked into the compiled binary; those require a rebuild. See Mobile Apps → Admin-configurable vs. rebuild for the exact list of which mobile values are which. Rule of thumb If you're not sure which bucket something falls in, check the settings reference first — if it's not listed there, it's a code change.

title: Installation Wizard Walkthrough
excerpt: Point your domain (or a subdirectory — see Subdirectory install) at script/public and visit it in a browser. Until the app is installed, every request redirects
text: Point your domain (or a subdirectory — see Subdirectory install) at script/public and visit it in a browser. Until the app is installed, every request redirects to /install; once installed, /install/* stops existing entirely (404) — there's no separate "delete the installer folder" step to remember. The wizard is safe to re-run or resume: nothing is written to your real database or .env until the final "Run" step, and that step itself is idempotent (safe to retry if it fails partway — migrations skip what's already applied, settings are upserted, not duplicated). The wizard has eight steps. Each one is shown below as it looks on a fresh install. 1. Welcome A short intro. Have your database name, username and password ready before you continue. 2. Requirements A read-only checklist: PHP ≥ 8.3 and the required extensions (pdo_mysql, mbstring, openssl, curl, zip, fileinfo, bcmath, intl, tokenizer, xml, plus either GD or Imagick). You can't continue until every required item is green — see Server requirements if something's missing. proc_open and symlink are checked too but don't block you; the wizard copies files instead if symlink() isn't available on your host. 3. Permissions Checks that storage/, bootstrap/cache/ and .env (or the app folder, if .env doesn't exist yet) are writable by the web server. If something is red, set that folder to 775 in your file manager or with chmod, then reload. 4. Database Host, port, database name, username and password. The database must already exist — create it first in cPanel → MySQL Databases (or your host's equivalent). When you press Continue the wizard opens a test connection; nothing is written yet. 5. Application Your site name, its full URL (no trailing slash), timezone, default language and default currency. More languages and currencies can be added later from Admin. 6. Admin account The first admin's name, email and password. This account is created already verified, so you can sign in straight away. 7. Run Press Run installation. The wizard writes .env, runs the migrations, seeds the database, applies your language and currency, creates your admin account and links storage. It usually takes under a minute. Every part is safe to retry if it fails partway. 8. Done You get your site and login links, plus the exact cron line to copy for your server — set it up now (see Cron & queue workers). Then sign in and continue in the Admin panel. Mail and storage come next The wizard doesn't ask for mail or file storage. The site works without them; set them up afterwards from Admin → Settings → Mail and Storage. The Admin overview reminds you until you do. How "installed" is tracked Two things both have to be true for the app to consider itself installed: a lock file at storage/app/installed.json, and a row in the installations table (install date and version). If either is missing, every request bounces back to the wizard.

title: Installing on cPanel / Shared Hosting
excerpt: PerfectEvents was specifically designed to work on ordinary shared hosting — no Composer, no Node, no SSH, no Supervisor. The default settings (QUEUE_CONNECTION
text: PerfectEvents was specifically designed to work on ordinary shared hosting — no Composer, no Node, no SSH, no Supervisor. The default settings (QUEUE_CONNECTION=database, SESSION_DRIVER=database, CACHE_STORE=database) exist for exactly this case. 1. Upload Upload the script/ folder's contents to your account (via File Manager's zip-upload or FTP). Most cPanel setups serve a domain from public_html/, but Laravel needs its web root to be script/public, not the app root. Two common ways to handle this: "Application root" hosting (recommended, if your host offers it) — some cPanel setups let you point the domain's document root directly at a subfolder. Upload everything to e.g. perfectevents/ outside public_html, and set the domain's document root to perfectevents/public. Manual split — upload everything to a folder above public_html (e.g. app/), then move only the contents of app/public into public_html, and edit public_html/index.php's two require paths to point up to ../app/vendor/autoload.php and ../app/bootstrap/app.php. 2. Create the database In cPanel → MySQL Databases: create a database, a user, and grant that user all privileges on the database. You'll enter these three values in the wizard's Database step. 3. Run the installer Visit your domain — you'll land on /install automatically. Follow the wizard walkthrough. 4. Add the cron entry cPanel → Cron Jobs → add a new job, run every minute: * * * * * php /home/youruser/perfectevents/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1 Use the full absolute path to your script/artisan file and whatever PHP binary your host provides for CLI (check with your host if php alone doesn't resolve to 8.3+ — many shared hosts need something like /usr/local/bin/php83). This single line covers everything scheduled — including keeping the queue moving; see Cron & queue workers for what actually runs off it. 5. HTTPS Enable AutoSSL (or your host's equivalent) and make sure APP_URL in .env uses https:// — the app tightens session-cookie security automatically once it does. See HTTPS. No SSH? No problem Everything above is doable entirely through cPanel's web UI. If you do have SSH, you can instead run php artisan migrate etc. manually, but nothing in this product requires it.

title: Installing on a VPS
excerpt: A VPS gives you two things shared hosting can't: root access, and the option of a persistent queue worker instead of relying purely on the once-a-minute cron dr
text: A VPS gives you two things shared hosting can't: root access, and the option of a persistent queue worker instead of relying purely on the once-a-minute cron drain. Nothing here is required — the shared-hosting-friendly defaults still work fine on a VPS — but if you want the lower-latency setup, this is it. 1. Base packages Nginx, PHP 8.3+ with the extensions in Server Requirements, MySQL 8.0+, Composer (only if you're rebuilding vendor/ yourself — not required if you kept the shipped vendor/ folder) 2. Deploy the code Clone/upload script/ to e.g. /var/www/perfectevents. Point Nginx's document root at /var/www/perfectevents/public: server { listen 80; server_name example.com; root /var/www/perfectevents/public; index index.php; location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string; } location ~ \.php$ { fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php8.3-fpm.sock; fastcgi_index index.php; include fastcgi_params; fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root$fastcgi_script_name; } location ~ /\.(?!well-known).* { deny all; } } Set ownership so the web server user can write to storage/ and bootstrap/cache/: chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/perfectevents/storage /var/www/perfectevents/bootstrap/cache 3. Create the database, run the wizard Create a MySQL 8 database and user, then visit your domain and follow the install wizard. 4. Cron (required either way) # crontab -e * * * * * php /var/www/perfectevents/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1 5. Optional: Supervisor-managed queue worker The scheduled queue:work --stop-when-empty --max-time=50 (riding on the cron line above) is enough for shared hosting. On a VPS you can run a persistent worker instead for lower latency on ticket emails/PDFs/pushes — both can coexist safely, the scheduled one just exits immediately if the queue's already empty. # /etc/supervisor/conf.d/perfectevents-worker.conf [program:perfectevents-worker] process_name=%(program_name)s_%(process_num)02d command=php /var/www/perfectevents/artisan queue:work --sleep=3 --tries=3 --max-time=3600 autostart=true autorestart=true numprocs=2 user=www-data stopwaitsecs=3600 supervisorctl reread supervisorctl update supervisorctl start perfectevents-worker:* 6. HTTPS Terminate TLS with Certbot/Let's Encrypt (or your load balancer), then set APP_URL=https://… — see HTTPS.

title: Installing in a Subdirectory
excerpt: PerfectEvents can run at a path like example.com/events instead of owning a whole domain, but the web server's document root still has to point at script/public
text: PerfectEvents can run at a path like example.com/events instead of owning a whole domain, but the web server's document root still has to point at script/public — you can't just drop the whole app folder inside your existing site's public folder and expect it to route correctly. Apache (cPanel-style) Create an "Addon Domain" or subdomain pointed at a folder, upload PerfectEvents there, and set that folder's document root to its public subfolder — same as a full domain install (see cPanel), just mapped under a path instead of the domain root. A true "subfolder of an existing document root" setup (e.g. an existing Apache vhost serving example.com, with PerfectEvents at /events underneath it) needs an Alias directive pointing /events at script/public, since Laravel's own routing has no concept of a URL prefix without one: Alias /events /var/www/perfectevents/public <Directory /var/www/perfectevents/public> AllowOverride All Require all granted </Directory> Nginx location /events { alias /var/www/perfectevents/public; try_files $uri $uri/ @events; } location @events { rewrite ^/events/(.*)$ /events/index.php?$1 last; } location ~ ^/events/index\.php$ { fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php8.3-fpm.sock; fastcgi_index index.php; include fastcgi_params; fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $document_root/index.php; fastcgi_param SCRIPT_NAME /events/index.php; } Set the app URL Whichever route you take, set APP_URL (in the wizard's Application step, or later in .env) to the full path including the subdirectory — https://example.com/events — so generated links, assets, and redirects come out correct. Simplest option If your host supports subdomains easily, a subdomain (events.example.com) avoids all of the rewrite-rule complexity above and is worth considering over a true subdirectory.

title: Troubleshooting the Installer
excerpt: The Requirements step won't turn green Symptom: One or more items on the Requirements screen stays red. Cause: A PHP extension is missing, or you're on PHP < 8.
text: The Requirements step won't turn green Symptom: One or more items on the Requirements screen stays red. Cause: A PHP extension is missing, or you're on PHP < 8.3. Fix: Check with your host how to enable the missing extension (cPanel: "MultiPHP INI Editor" or "Select PHP Version" → extension checkboxes; VPS: apt install php8.3-<ext> then restart PHP-FPM). Either GD or Imagick satisfies the image requirement — you don't need both. The Permissions step won't turn green Symptom: storage/, bootstrap/cache/, or .env shows as not writable. Cause: Upload tools sometimes preserve restrictive permissions, or the web server runs as a different user than the one that uploaded the files. Fix: chmod -R 775 storage bootstrap/cache (or 755, depending on your host's ownership model), and make sure the folder containing .env is writable if .env doesn't exist yet. On shared hosting, re-uploading via File Manager rather than FTP sometimes fixes ownership mismatches outright. "Test connection" fails on the Database step Symptom: Database step won't proceed even with correct-looking credentials. Cause: Almost always one of: wrong host (shared hosting is often localhost, not 127.0.0.1, or vice versa), the database user hasn't been granted privileges on that specific database yet, or the DB name/user needed your cPanel account's prefix (e.g. cpaneluser_dbname). Fix: Double-check the exact values from cPanel → MySQL Databases, including the prefix. On a VPS, confirm mysql -u youruser -p -h host database works from the same server first. "Send test email" fails on the Mail step Symptom: Test email never arrives, or the button shows an error. Cause: Wrong port/encryption combination is the most common one — port 587 wants tls, port 465 wants ssl. Some hosts also block outbound port 25/587 entirely. Fix: Confirm the port+encryption pairing with your mail provider. You can also just skip this for now (leave the driver as log) and configure real SMTP later from Admin → Settings → Mail — it isn't required to finish installing. Blank page / 500 error after finishing the wizard Symptom: The Done screen never appears; you get a blank page or a generic server error. Cause: Usually a PHP error during the Run step's migration/seed — check your host's PHP error log (cPanel: "Errors" in the file manager, or storage/logs/laravel.log if it got far enough to write one). Fix: The Run step is safe to retry — fix whatever the log points at (commonly a missing extension that Requirements somehow didn't catch, or a database privilege gap) and reload /install; it'll resume from wherever it left off rather than starting over. Installed site redirects back to /install Symptom: Visiting your domain after a successful install redirects back to /install. Cause: The install lock (storage/app/installed.json) was deleted — often by a "clean" redeploy that didn't preserve the storage/ folder, or by a backup restore that only restored the database and not the filesystem. Fix: Since your installations database row is likely still intact, don't re-run the full wizard (it would try to re-seed). Restore storage/app/installed.json from a backup if you have one; if not, this is a support-ticket situation rather than something to work around by hand. Still stuck? See the full troubleshooting index for issues outside the installer itself.

title: Post-Install Security Checklist
excerpt: Most of the hardening below ships on by default — nothing to configure. This page is mainly about the few things that depend on your environment. Already handle
text: Most of the hardening below ships on by default — nothing to configure. This page is mainly about the few things that depend on your environment. Already handled for you Security headers on every response — Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and Strict-Transport-Security whenever the request is HTTPS. Rich-text sanitization — CMS page bodies and FAQ answers are sanitized on save; an admin account being compromised (or a copy-pasted body with embedded script) can't turn into stored XSS. Upload type restrictions — logo, favicon, organizer logo, and event cover/gallery uploads are restricted to JPEG/PNG/GIF/WebP; SVG is deliberately excluded everywhere uploads are accepted, since an SVG can carry a script. Rate limiting — public search/discovery endpoints and the whole API have floor-level throttles against scraping and brute-force abuse. Signed, verified webhooks — every payment gateway's webhook is signature- and amount-checked before it's trusted; a webhook URL alone is never enough to fake a payment. Signed QR tickets — ticket QR codes are HMAC-signed; the scanner rejects a forged or altered code even if someone guesses a ticket's code format. Email verification gates checkout for self-registered accounts. Things you need to set yourself Use HTTPS. Enable AutoSSL/Let's Encrypt and set APP_URL to https:// — the app automatically enables secure session cookies and HSTS once it sees that. Running over plain HTTP after launch is the single biggest gap on this list. See HTTPS. Use a strong admin password. The install wizard enforces a 10-character minimum on the admin account it creates, but a long, unique password (ideally from a password manager) is on you. Keep gateway credentials to live keys only in production. Double-check each payment gateway is switched from its test/sandbox mode to live mode (Admin → Settings → Payment gateways) before you actually launch — see Integrations for each gateway's specific keys. Turn on SMTP for real mail delivery. If you left the Mail step on the `log` driver during install, transactional emails (password resets, ticket receipts, verification links) are only being written to a log file, not delivered. Set real SMTP from Admin → Settings → Mail. Restrict database credentials. Use a MySQL user scoped to only the PerfectEvents database, not a shared root-equivalent account. Keep automated backups. There's no built-in backup feature yet (see Backups) — set up your host's or provider's own scheduled MySQL dump + file backup for storage/app/public (uploaded media) if you don't already have one. A known, deliberate trade-off The default Content-Security-Policy allows unsafe-eval/unsafe-inline in script-src because the Admin/Organizer panels use Alpine.js (via Livewire), which evaluates inline expressions. The policy still meaningfully restricts framing, object embeds, and form submission targets — it isn't a no-op — but it isn't a maximally strict CSP either. This is an intentional limit of the hand-rolled-panel architecture, not an oversight.

title: Environment Variables
excerpt: Most buyer-facing configuration — payment gateway keys, SMS, social login, branding, SEO — lives in the database and is edited from Admin → Settings, not .env.
text: Most buyer-facing configuration — payment gateway keys, SMS, social login, branding, SEO — lives in the database and is edited from Admin → Settings, not .env. See the full settings reference for that half. .env covers framework-level and bootstrap-time configuration: things the app needs before it can even reach the database. Application VariablePurpose APP_NAMEInitial display name — Admin → Settings → Branding overrides it at runtime. APP_ENVproduction on a real install (the installer sets this). APP_KEYLaravel's encryption key. Generated automatically during install — never share it or commit it. APP_DEBUGMust be false in production — the installer forces this. APP_URLYour site's base URL, including https://. Used to generate absolute links, assets, and webhook URLs. APP_TIMEZONEPlatform default timezone — overridable at runtime from Admin → Settings → General, which then wins. APP_LOCALE / APP_FALLBACK_LOCALEDefault and fallback UI locale. Database DB_CONNECTION (always mysql — MySQL 8.0+ only), DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_DATABASE, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD — all set by the installer's Database step. Session, queue, cache SESSION_DRIVER, QUEUE_CONNECTION, and CACHE_STORE all default to database — deliberately, so nothing requires Redis or a service beyond MySQL on shared hosting. See Cache and Cron & queue workers if you want to opt into Redis on a VPS. Mail (bootstrap defaults only) MAIL_MAILER, MAIL_HOST, MAIL_PORT, MAIL_USERNAME, MAIL_PASSWORD, MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS, MAIL_FROM_NAME. These only seed the installer's Mail step — once installed, the live values you edit from Admin → Settings → Mail take over and .env is no longer consulted. Storage / S3 (bootstrap defaults only) FILESYSTEM_DISK, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, AWS_BUCKET, AWS_USE_PATH_STYLE_ENDPOINT. Same pattern as Mail — see Storage / S3. Not in .env.example — add these yourself if you need them VariablePurpose FCM_CREDENTIALSFilesystem path to your Firebase service-account JSON — required for mobile push notifications. See Firebase & push. FCM_PROJECT_IDOptional override; normally read straight from the service-account file. PERFECT_EVENTS_DEMO_MODENever set this on a real install. It's exclusively for a live CodeCanyon-style public demo — it enables demo data reset and locks the shared demo admin account's own credentials. Never commit .env It contains your database password and app encryption key. It's excluded from the zip and should never be committed to a git repo you push publicly.

title: Cron & Queue Workers
excerpt: There's exactly one hard requirement: a standard Laravel scheduler cron entry, once a minute. * * * * * php /path/to/script/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>
text: There's exactly one hard requirement: a standard Laravel scheduler cron entry, once a minute. * * * * * php /path/to/script/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1 Until the cron runs, Admin → Overview shows Scheduler (cron): Not detected under Needs attention. What rides on that one line JobFrequencyWhat it does orders:release-expiredEvery minuteCancels pending orders past their payment-hold deadline and returns inventory to sale. queue:work --stop-when-empty --max-time=50Every minuteKeeps the queue moving — ticket PDFs, emails, image conversions, and push notifications are all queued jobs. This is what makes a dedicated worker process optional; it exits immediately once the queue's empty, and it re-runs every minute either way. events:send-remindersEvery 15 minutesSends 24-hour and 1-hour reminders before an event; safe to run this often, dedup is tracked per-reminder. activity-log:pruneDailyTrims the audit log according to your configured retention period (no-ops if you haven't set one). Cron heartbeatEvery minuteRecords a timestamp Admin → System reads to tell you whether cron is actually running. If Admin → System shows a stale heartbeat, your cron entry isn't firing — check the exact PHP path/version your host's cron uses (see Troubleshooting the installer for the same PHP-binary-path issue at install time). Optional: a persistent queue worker (VPS + Supervisor) On a VPS, you can run a long-lived worker for lower latency on ticket emails/PDFs than waiting for the once-a-minute cron drain. Both can run at the same time safely — see Installing on a VPS for the Supervisor config. On shared hosting without SSH, skip this entirely; the cron-driven drain is what the defaults are built around. Redis is optional, not required QUEUE_CONNECTION, CACHE_STORE, and SESSION_DRIVER all default to database so nothing beyond MySQL is required. If you're on a VPS and want Redis for throughput, it's a drop-in .env change — nothing in the app assumes one driver over the other.

title: Storage & S3
excerpt: Event covers, organizer logos, branding assets, and generated ticket PDFs all go through Laravel's filesystem abstraction, so switching between local disk and S
text: Event covers, organizer logos, branding assets, and generated ticket PDFs all go through Laravel's filesystem abstraction, so switching between local disk and S3 doesn't change how anything in the app behaves. Admin → Settings → Storage Local disk (default) Files are stored under storage/app/public and served via the storage:link symlink the installer creates automatically. No further setup — this is what a fresh install uses unless you choose S3 during the wizard's Storage step. Switching to S3 From Admin → Settings → Storage (or during the install wizard's Storage step), switch the driver to S3 and provide: FieldNotes Access key / secretAn IAM user scoped to just this bucket is safer than reusing broad account credentials. Regione.g. us-east-1 BucketMust already exist — the app doesn't create it for you. Endpoint / URLOptional — only needed for an S3-compatible provider (DigitalOcean Spaces, Cloudflare R2, MinIO) instead of AWS itself. Use the "test storage" button on that screen before saving — it writes, reads, and deletes a temp object, so a bad key/bucket/permission combination is caught immediately instead of failing silently on the next real upload. Media library also follows this setting Event/organizer image conversions (thumbnails, cards, covers) are generated by the media library package, which automatically switches to your S3 disk the moment you enable it — no separate configuration for "where do thumbnails go." Bucket policy for S3 Uploaded media (event covers, logos, branding assets) needs to be publicly readable for the site to display it. Ticket PDFs are different: they're written to the same disk but only ever served through an authenticated API route that streams the file through the app after checking the requester actually owns the order — so the bucket doesn't need to allow public reads for ticket delivery to work, and a stored PDF isn't reachable by guessing its URL.

title: Cache
excerpt: CACHE_STORE=database is the default — no Redis/Memcached required. Several parts of the app cache automatically and invalidate themselves the moment the underly
text: CACHE_STORE=database is the default — no Redis/Memcached required. Several parts of the app cache automatically and invalidate themselves the moment the underlying data changes, so there's nothing to manually clear after normal editing: Public listing pages (home, category, organizer, city, event search) are cached briefly and invalidated the instant an event is created, published, or updated. Reference data (active categories, currencies, languages) is cached until changed. The computed settings payload (everything Admin → Settings controls) is cached until the next settings save. Translation overrides are cached per-locale, invalidated on save. When you might need to clear it manually Admin → System has a "clear cache" button for the rare case something looks stale after a direct database change (a manual SQL fix, a restored backup) rather than a normal edit through the panel. Day to day, you shouldn't need it. Opting into Redis If you're on a VPS and want Redis for cache/session/queue instead of the database driver, it's a plain .env swap (CACHE_STORE=redis, REDIS_HOST, etc.) — nothing in the app assumes one driver over the other. Not required for any deployment size this product is built for; the database driver scales fine for a single-server install.

title: HTTPS
excerpt: Running without HTTPS is fine for local testing, but not for a real launch — payment gateways, OAuth social login, and browser geolocation/push APIs either requ
text: Running without HTTPS is fine for local testing, but not for a real launch — payment gateways, OAuth social login, and browser geolocation/push APIs either require it outright or degrade without it. Getting a certificate Shared hosting (cPanel) — enable AutoSSL under SSL/TLS Status; most hosts issue a free Let's Encrypt certificate automatically once your domain resolves correctly. VPS — Certbot (certbot --nginx) is the simplest path, or terminate TLS at a load balancer/CDN in front of the app. Tell the app about it Set APP_URL=https://yourdomain.com (no trailing slash) in .env. Once the app sees an HTTPS APP_URL, two things change automatically: Session cookies are marked Secure (won't be sent over plain HTTP). The Strict-Transport-Security header is added to every response, instructing browsers to never downgrade back to HTTP for your domain. Mixed content If you switch an existing HTTP install to HTTPS after uploads already exist, double check any stored absolute URLs (a custom CMS block with a hardcoded http:// image link, for example) — generated links from the app itself always follow APP_URL, but content an admin typed in by hand won't rewrite itself.

title: Stripe
excerpt: Configured entirely from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → Stripe — no .env changes needed. Admin → Settings → Payment gateways. Save the keys, press Test c
text: Configured entirely from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → Stripe — no .env changes needed. Admin → Settings → Payment gateways. Save the keys, press Test connection, then switch the gateway on. Keys you need FieldWhere to find it Secret keyStripe Dashboard → Developers → API keys. Starts with sk_test_ or sk_live_. Publishable keySame screen, starts with pk_test_/pk_live_ — used client-side, safe to expose. Webhook signing secretCreated when you register the webhook endpoint below — starts with whsec_. Webhook URL In Stripe Dashboard → Developers → Webhooks, add an endpoint: https://yourdomain.com/api/v1/webhooks/stripe Subscribe it to at least payment_intent.succeeded and payment_intent.payment_failed. Copy the signing secret it gives you into the Webhook signing secret field in Admin. In the mobile app The customer app pays with Stripe's own in-app payment sheet — cards, plus Apple Pay / Google Pay where the device supports them — so buyers never leave the app. It uses the publishable key above; nothing else to set up in the app. The order is confirmed by the webhook, exactly as on the website. Test mode Use your sk_test_/pk_test_ keys and Stripe's published test card numbers (e.g. 4242 4242 4242 4242, any future expiry, any CVC — see Stripe's own testing docs for the full set including 3D Secure and decline scenarios). Switch to sk_live_/pk_live_ — and re-register a live-mode webhook endpoint, Stripe keeps test and live webhooks separate — before accepting real payments. Verify before you launch Use the "test" button next to the gateway in Admin — it validates your keys can actually reach Stripe before you flip the gateway to enabled.

title: PayPal
excerpt: Configured from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → PayPal. Keys you need FieldNotes Modesandbox or live — this is PayPal's test-mode toggle, there's no separ
text: Configured from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → PayPal. Keys you need FieldNotes Modesandbox or live — this is PayPal's test-mode toggle, there's no separate test key pair. Client ID / Client secretFrom your PayPal Developer Dashboard app — sandbox and live apps have separate credentials. Webhook IDCreated when you register the webhook below. Webhook URL https://yourdomain.com/api/v1/webhooks/paypal Register this in your PayPal app's Webhooks settings, subscribed to at minimum CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED — that event is what actually triggers the payment capture server-side, so checkout only ever resolves through one settled event rather than trusting the client's redirect alone. How the flow works The buyer is redirected to PayPal to approve the order; PayPal's webhook firing CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED is what the platform actually captures against — the redirect back to your site is a UX convenience, not the trust boundary. Test mode Use sandbox mode with a PayPal sandbox buyer account (create one from the Developer Dashboard → Sandbox → Accounts). Switch to live — with your live app's client ID/secret and a live-registered webhook — before launch.

title: Razorpay
excerpt: Configured from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → Razorpay. Keys you need FieldWhere to find it Key IDRazorpay Dashboard → Settings → API Keys. Public, used
text: Configured from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → Razorpay. Keys you need FieldWhere to find it Key IDRazorpay Dashboard → Settings → API Keys. Public, used client-side. Key secretSame screen — keep this one server-side only. Webhook secretSet when you create the webhook below. Webhook URL https://yourdomain.com/api/v1/webhooks/razorpay Add this under Dashboard → Settings → Webhooks, subscribed to at least payment.captured and payment.failed (order.paid is also treated as a success signal). Set a webhook secret there and enter the same value in Admin — every webhook is HMAC-verified against it before it's trusted. How the flow works The app creates a Razorpay Order server-side, then opens Razorpay Checkout — on the website, or natively inside the customer app — with that order id and your public key ID. The buyer never sees your key secret, and the order is confirmed by the webhook either way. A payment finished outside the app (some UPI or wallet apps) is picked up the same way. Test mode Razorpay test/live mode is switched from within the Razorpay Dashboard itself (a toggle at account level), each with its own key pair — enter whichever pair matches the mode you're currently in. See Razorpay's own docs for current test card/UPI numbers.

title: Paystack
excerpt: Configured from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → Paystack. Keys you need Just one: your secret key, from Paystack Dashboard → Settings → API Keys & Webhook
text: Configured from Admin → Settings → Payment gateways → Paystack. Keys you need Just one: your secret key, from Paystack Dashboard → Settings → API Keys & Webhooks. Starts with sk_test_ or sk_live_ depending on mode — which key you enter is the test/live toggle, there's no separate mode field. Webhook URL https://yourdomain.com/api/v1/webhooks/paystack Set this under the same API Keys & Webhooks screen. Paystack signs every webhook with your secret key itself (HMAC-SHA512) rather than a separate webhook secret, so there's nothing extra to copy in beyond the secret key above. How the flow works Checkout is a hosted redirect: the app initializes a transaction server-side and sends the buyer to the authorization_url Paystack returns. The webhook (charge.success / charge.failed) is what confirms the payment. Test mode Use a sk_test_ key and Paystack's published test card numbers. Swap to a sk_live_ key before launch — remember to also update the webhook URL/key pairing if you're using separate Paystack integrations for test vs. live.

title: Email (SMTP)
excerpt: Set from Admin → Settings → Mail (or the install wizard's Mail step, which seeds the same fields). Used for: email verification links, password resets, order re
text: Set from Admin → Settings → Mail (or the install wizard's Mail step, which seeds the same fields). Used for: email verification links, password resets, order receipts and ticket delivery, event reminders, and refund/payout notifications. Fields FieldNotes Driversmtp for real delivery; log writes emails to the log file instead of sending (useful only while testing, never for a live site). Host / PortYour provider's SMTP hostname and port — see common pairings below. Encryptiontls for port 587, ssl for port 465. Username / PasswordYour SMTP account credentials — for API-based providers (see below) this is usually a fixed username plus an API key as the password. From address / From nameWhat recipients see as the sender. Use the "send test email" button before relying on it — a bad host/port/encryption combination otherwise fails silently until a real customer doesn't get their tickets. Common providers ProviderHostPort / Encryption Gmail / Google Workspacesmtp.gmail.com587 / tls (requires an app password, not your account password) SendGridsmtp.sendgrid.net587 / tls (username is literally apikey) Mailgunsmtp.mailgun.org587 / tls Amazon SESemail-smtp.<region>.amazonaws.com587 / tls Your host's own mail servere.g. mail.yourdomain.com587 / tls or 465 / ssl — check with your host Set up SPF/DKIM with your provider This is outside the app's control, but without it, a meaningful share of transactional email (including ticket delivery) ends up in spam. Follow your SMTP provider's domain-verification steps.

title: SMS (Twilio)
excerpt: SMS is off by default. If you turn it on from Admin → Settings → SMS, Twilio is the only supported provider. Fields FieldWhere to find it EnabledThe master on/o
text: SMS is off by default. If you turn it on from Admin → Settings → SMS, Twilio is the only supported provider. Fields FieldWhere to find it EnabledThe master on/off switch for the whole SMS channel. Account SIDTwilio Console dashboard. Auth tokenSame screen — treat it like a password. From numberA Twilio phone number capable of sending SMS in your target countries. Use the "send test SMS" button to confirm the number and credentials actually work before relying on it. What actually sends an SMS today Turning this channel on enables SMS delivery for ticket-issued notifications specifically — buyers get a text when their tickets are ready, in addition to email. It isn't a general-purpose SMS channel for every notification type yet. Costs money per message Twilio bills per SMS sent, and rates vary a lot by destination country — check Twilio's pricing for the countries your buyers are actually in before turning this on for a high-volume event.

title: Social Login
excerpt: Configured per-provider from Admin → Settings → Social login. Three providers are supported: Google, Apple, Facebook — each with its own enable switch and its o
text: Configured per-provider from Admin → Settings → Social login. Three providers are supported: Google, Apple, Facebook — each with its own enable switch and its own client ID/secret. Fields (per provider) FieldNotes EnabledTurns the login button on/off on the site and in the apps for that provider specifically. Client IDFrom the provider's own developer console. Client secretSame place — keep it private. Redirect / callback URL to register with each provider https://yourdomain.com/auth/{provider}/callback Substitute google, apple, or facebook for {provider}. Register this exact URL in each provider's console (Google Cloud Console → Credentials; Apple Developer → Sign in with Apple; Meta for Developers → Facebook Login) or the callback will fail with a redirect-URI-mismatch error. How linking works A social sign-in is matched to an existing account by email address if one already exists (so a buyer who registered with email/password and later clicks "Continue with Google" using the same address links to the same account, rather than creating a duplicate), and creates a new account otherwise. Apple has extra requirements "Sign in with Apple" requires your own Apple Developer account, a registered Services ID, and a generated private key/JWT for client secret rotation — Apple's setup has more moving parts than Google or Facebook. Follow Apple's own Sign in with Apple documentation for generating those credentials; what you paste into Admin is the same client ID / secret concept either way.

title: Firebase & Push Notifications
excerpt: Push notifications need setup in two places: the Laravel server (to send pushes) and each Flutter app (to receive them). Neither is required for the rest of the
text: Push notifications need setup in two places: the Laravel server (to send pushes) and each Flutter app (to receive them). Neither is required for the rest of the product to work — push is an optional channel, off by default. 1. Server side (Laravel) In the Firebase console, open your project → Project settings → Service accounts, and generate a new private key. This downloads a JSON file. Upload that JSON file somewhere on your server outside the public web root, and add its path to .env: FCM_CREDENTIALS=/absolute/path/to/firebase-service-account.json Optionally set FCM_PROJECT_ID if you want to override the project id — normally it's read straight from the service-account file, so this is rarely needed. Turn the push channel on (alongside SMS/email) in notification settings. If the credentials file is missing or unreadable, the app doesn't error — it simply treats push as unconfigured and skips that channel silently, so a half-finished setup never breaks anything else. 2. Each Flutter app needs its own Firebase project The customer app and the scanner app are separate Firebase projects (or at minimum separate registered apps within one project) — set each one up independently via the FlutterFire CLI or the Firebase console: AppAndroid fileiOS file Customerflutter/apps/customer/android/app/google-services.jsonflutter/apps/customer/ios/Runner/GoogleService-Info.plist Scannerflutter/apps/scanner/android/app/google-services.jsonflutter/apps/scanner/ios/Runner/GoogleService-Info.plist The repo ships with placeholder Firebase config for its own demo project — replace both files per app with your own before building for release. This is one of the values that requires a rebuild, not an Admin setting — see Admin-configurable vs. rebuild. Test before you ship Send a test push to a debug build of each app once its config files are in place, before doing a release build — a wrong package name/bundle id in Firebase vs. the app itself is the most common reason pushes silently never arrive.

title: Admin Panel Tour
excerpt: The Admin panel (/admin) is for the platform owner — settings, moderation, and oversight across every organizer. It's a separate area from the Organizer panel;
text: The Admin panel (/admin) is for the platform owner — settings, moderation, and oversight across every organizer. It's a separate area from the Organizer panel; an admin account can see everything, an organizer only their own. Overview The first screen after login shows how the whole platform is doing. Pick a period (last 7, 30 or 90 days, or 12 months) at the top right; every figure and chart follows it. Headline numbers: gross sales, platform fees, paid orders, tickets sold, and attendance (the share of tickets checked in at events held in the period). Each shows the change against the previous period of the same length, plus a small trend line. Sales trend: gross sales and platform fees over the period. Needs attention: anything waiting on you, such as events and organizer applications to approve, reviews to moderate, failed background jobs, a scheduler (cron) that isn't running, oversold orders, or mail and storage settings you haven't configured yet. Upcoming events with how full each one is, and top events by gross sales. Tickets by category, where the money goes (how gross sales split into the organizers' share, platform fees, and tax added at checkout), and recent activity (orders, new events, sign-ups). Multiple currencies: PerfectEvents never converts between currencies, so money figures show one currency at a time. When you've sold in more than one, a currency switcher appears next to the period picker; it lists only currencies with sales and starts on your default currency. Order, ticket and attendance counts always include every currency. Events Every event across every organizer. This is where event approvals happen — a newly submitted event sits as "Pending" here until you approve or send it back with a note. Organizers Every organizer account, and where the other approval layer lives — reviewing a new organizer's application and approving, rejecting, or later suspending them. See Approvals for how this differs from event approval. Users Every account on the platform (customers, organizers, admins) — search, view, and manage individual accounts. Reviews Moderate buyer reviews left on events, if auto-approval is off (General settings). Orders, Refunds, Payouts Orders lists every order platform-wide with the ability to drill into one and issue a refund. Payouts is where organizer payout requests queue up for you to mark paid or reject. Coupons Platform-level coupon management, alongside whatever coupons individual organizers create for their own events — see Coupons. Roles & permissions Toggle which of the wireable permissions (event approval, settings management, payout approval, plus what organizers/staff can do) are granted to each role. See the permissions matrix for the full picture. CMS: Pages, FAQ, Banners, Homepage, Menus Static content pages, an FAQ list, promotional banners, the homepage's section layout, and header/footer menu items — see CMS & homepage. Categories, Venues, Currencies, Countries Reference data used throughout the platform: event categories, reusable venues, which currencies are active, and which countries are selectable in forms. Notification templates Edit the copy sent for each notification type — see Notification templates. Languages & Translations Add a language and translate UI chrome strings — see Localization. Settings Branding, general/tax/payout defaults, mail, storage, payment gateways, SMS, social login, and SEO — every buyer-configurable knob in the product lives here. Full list in the settings reference. Settings → Branding: your logo, favicon and colours. System A read-only operations page: PHP/Laravel versions and the same requirement checklist the installer used, queue health (pending/failed job counts, last 5 failures), whether cron is actually running (a heartbeat timestamp), disk usage, and a tail of recent error-level log lines. Also has a "clear cache" button and the maintenance-mode toggle — turning maintenance mode on takes the public site offline while leaving the

title: Organizer Panel Tour
excerpt: The Organizer panel (/organizer) is scoped: an organizer only ever sees their own events, orders, and staff — never another organizer's data. Dashboard The same
text: The Organizer panel (/organizer) is scoped: an organizer only ever sees their own events, orders, and staff — never another organizer's data. Dashboard The same analytics as the admin Overview, covering only the organizer's own events, with the same period picker and currency switcher. It shows gross sales and their own earnings, paid orders, tickets sold, attendance, a sales trend, upcoming events with how full each one is, top events, tickets by ticket type, how their sales split into earnings, service fees and tax, and recent orders and reviews. An At a glance card lists what they can act on: the balance available to withdraw (per currency), events waiting for approval, drafts, reviews awaiting a reply, and today's check-ins. Until they create their first event, the dashboard shows a single "Create event" prompt instead. Events Create and edit events — details, ticket types and pricing, venue, media, and publishing. A new or edited event goes to Pending status when submitted and needs admin approval before it's publicly visible; it doesn't go live the moment an organizer hits save. Events → New event walks through five steps: Basics, Schedule, Tickets, Details, Review. Orders Every order against their own events, with the ability to issue a refund on a paid order (subject to the platform's refund window setting) directly from here — the same underlying refund action an admin can also use. Attendees A searchable list of everyone who's bought a ticket to one of their events, with check-in status — useful for door-day headcounts without needing the scanner app open. Coupons Create discount codes scoped to their own events — see Coupons. Staff Add staff accounts (door/scanning-only access — no financial or settings visibility) and assign them to specific events for check-in duty. Reviews Buyer reviews left on their events — moderate/respond depending on whether auto-approval is on (a platform-wide setting; see the settings reference). Notifications Their own notification history/preferences — separate from the platform-wide notification templates an admin edits (see Notification templates). Payouts See their current available balance and request a payout against it; requests queue up for the admin to mark paid or reject. See Payouts for how the balance is calculated. Profile / account settings Name, email, password, two-factor authentication, and organizer profile details (bio, logo, a per-organizer commission override if one's been set for them).

title: Approvals
excerpt: There are two independent things an admin approves: whether someone is allowed to operate as an organizer at all, and whether a given event is allowed to go liv
text: There are two independent things an admin approves: whether someone is allowed to operate as an organizer at all, and whether a given event is allowed to go live. Approving one doesn't approve the other. Organizer account approval A new organizer account starts in Pending review. While pending, they can build and edit event drafts, but can't publish anything or appear on the public site. An admin reviews and sets the account to Approved (cleared to operate), Rejected, or later Suspended if an already-approved organizer needs to be pulled. Event approval Separately, each event moves through Draft (organizer still editing) → Pending (submitted, awaiting you) → Published (live and publicly discoverable), plus Cancelled and Completed once it's run its course or been called off. Only Published events are visible to buyers. Whether a submitted event actually needs your review is itself a Admin setting — "Require event approval" (General settings, on by default). With it on, every newly submitted event lands in Pending; with it off, submitting an event publishes it immediately, and this whole page mostly doesn't apply. Either way, an organizer who isn't yet account-approved can't publish at all, regardless of this setting. Reviewing a pending event Admin → Events, filtered to Pending, shows the listing exactly as the organizer built it — details, ticket types, pricing, venue, media. From there: Approve — publishes it immediately and clears any earlier moderation note. Send back to draft — requires a reason, stored on the event and shown to the organizer so they know what to fix. This also works on an already-live event, for pulling one back if a problem turns up after the fact. Editing an event that's already Published does not revert it to Pending — it stays published straight through the edit. Moderation is a one-time gate on getting live in the first place, not a re-review on every change. Featuring an event Independently of approval, an admin can mark any event as featured, used for homepage/featured placements. This has no bearing on whether the event is approved or public.

title: Refunds
excerpt: Refunds are issued from an order's detail page — either the Admin or Organizer panel, same underlying action either way (an organizer can refund their own order
text: Refunds are issued from an order's detail page — either the Admin or Organizer panel, same underlying action either way (an organizer can refund their own orders without needing an admin). What a refund does Calls the original payment gateway to actually return the money. Records a refund row against the order. Releases the order's ticket inventory and coupon redemption back to sale. Voids the order's tickets (they stop scanning as valid) and notifies the buyer. Every refund is written to the audit log automatically — no separate step, and no way to issue one that doesn't get logged, regardless of whether it came from the Admin panel, the Organizer panel, or the API directly. What can be refunded Only a paid order (or one already partially refunded) is eligible. Refunds are whole-order only in this version — there's no partial/per-ticket refund yet, so if a buyer wants to return 2 of 4 tickets, that's a manual conversation outside the tool for now. The refund window Admin → Settings → General has a refund window (in days; 0 means unlimited). Once an order is older than that window, refunding it through the panel is blocked — this exists to stop a refund being issued for an event that's already happened and been attended. Refunds and checked-in tickets Refunding an order voids its tickets. If someone's already been scanned in at the door and you refund their order afterward, their ticket becomes invalid retroactively — make sure that's the outcome you actually want before refunding a same-day order.

title: Payouts
excerpt: There's no automated money movement to organizers in this version. Payouts are a tracking and request workflow: the platform calculates what an organizer is owe
text: There's no automated money movement to organizers in this version. Payouts are a tracking and request workflow: the platform calculates what an organizer is owed, the organizer requests a payout against that balance, and an admin marks it paid once they've actually sent the money by whatever means (bank transfer, PayPal, etc.) outside the platform. How the balance is calculated For every paid order against an organizer's events, the order's payable amount already has the platform fee deducted (when the organizer is the fee payer). On top of that, a commission percentage is applied at payout time — either a per-organizer override (set on their profile) or the platform default (Admin → Settings → General). Balances are tracked per currency separately, since one organizer can run events priced in more than one currency. Available balance = net earnings to date, minus payouts already requested or paid. A rejected request frees that amount back up. The organizer side Organizer → Payouts shows their current available balance per currency, with a "request payout" action — they choose an amount up to what's available (with an optional note) and it goes into a Pending queue. The admin side Admin → Payouts lists every pending request across all organizers. For each one: Mark paid — with a reference (e.g. a bank transfer id), once you've actually sent the money. Reject — with a note explaining why; the requested amount becomes available to request again. Either action notifies the organizer. This is a ledger, not a payment processor Nothing here initiates a bank transfer or PayPal payout automatically — "mark paid" is you confirming a payment you made yourself elsewhere. Building that connection to an actual payout processor (Stripe Connect, PayPal Payouts, etc.) is not part of this version.

title: Coupons
excerpt: Both admins and organizers can create coupons — an organizer's are scoped to their own events; an admin can create platform-level ones. A coupon is either scope
text: Both admins and organizers can create coupons — an organizer's are scoped to their own events; an admin can create platform-level ones. A coupon is either scoped to one specific event or to every event by an organizer, whichever fits. Discount types TypeHow it's applied PercentA whole-number percent off the order subtotal (e.g. 10 = 10% off), capped at 100%. FixedA flat amount off, in your currency's minor units — capped at the subtotal, so a coupon can never push an order negative. Eligibility rules A coupon fields all of the following before it's allowed to apply, checked at the moment of checkout: Active — the coupon's own on/off switch. Start date — if set, the coupon isn't usable before it. End date — if set, the coupon isn't usable after it. Max redemptions — if set, the coupon stops working once it's been used that many times total. Minimum order amount — if set, the order subtotal has to meet it for the coupon to apply. What happens with an ineligible code If a buyer enters a code that fails one of the rules above, checkout doesn't reject the order — it simply proceeds at full price without the discount. There's no error message blocking the purchase over a bad/expired coupon code; the buyer just doesn't get the discount they expected, so it's worth communicating coupon terms clearly wherever you advertise a code. Tracking redemptions Each coupon tracks how many times it's been redeemed, which is what the max-redemptions limit checks against. A refunded order that used a coupon releases that redemption back — see Refunds.

title: CMS & Homepage
excerpt: Pages Static content pages (About, Terms, Privacy, etc.) with a rich-text editor. Content is sanitized on save, so pasted HTML can't be used to inject scripts.
text: Pages Static content pages (About, Terms, Privacy, etc.) with a rich-text editor. Content is sanitized on save, so pasted HTML can't be used to inject scripts. FAQ A flat list of question/answer entries, shown on a public FAQ page and linked from the troubleshooting/support surfaces of the site. Banners Promotional banner images/links, shown wherever the Banners homepage section is placed (see below) — add, reorder, and set an optional link per banner. Menus Header/footer navigation items — add links to pages, categories, or external URLs, and control their order. Homepage sections The homepage is built from a fixed set of section types — Banners, Featured (events), Upcoming (events), Categories — that you arrange and toggle on/off, rather than a free-form page builder. Each section type pulls its own data live (Featured always shows currently-featured events, Upcoming always shows what's coming up), so there's nothing to keep manually in sync as events change. Not a drag-and-drop page builder You're arranging and configuring instances of these four section types, not building arbitrary custom layouts block-by-block. For anything beyond what a section type offers, that's a code change — see Admin vs. rebuild.

title: Notification Templates
excerpt: The platform sends 15 kinds of notification — order placed, tickets issued, payment failed, event reminders, refunds, payouts, and more — each potentially over
text: The platform sends 15 kinds of notification — order placed, tickets issued, payment failed, event reminders, refunds, payouts, and more — each potentially over multiple channels (email, in-app, push, SMS) and in multiple languages. Admin → Notification templates is where you edit the actual wording for each. How a template is identified Every template row is keyed by (notification key, channel, locale) — for example, "Payment successful + tickets" over "mail" in "es" is a different row from the same notification over "push", or the same channel in "en". You edit subject and body per row, and can turn any individual row off (falls back to the platform's built-in default text if you deactivate a custom one, so it's safe to try a rewrite without risking a broken/empty notification going out). Placeholders Each notification type supports a fixed set of {{placeholder}} tokens you can use in your subject/body — for example the tickets-issued email supports {{buyer_name}}, {{event_title}}, and {{ticket_count}}. The editor tells you which placeholders are valid for the row you're editing; an unrecognized token is just left as literal text rather than silently failing. Which channels each notification can use Not every notification supports every channel — order-placed, for instance, doesn't go out over SMS, only tickets-issued does (SMS also has to be turned on separately — see SMS — before any SMS row can actually deliver). The editor only shows channel rows that notification type actually supports. This is wording, not workflow You're editing what a notification says, not adding new kinds of notification or new trigger conditions — the set of 15 keys is fixed. Adding a genuinely new notification type is a code change.

title: Localization & Adding a Language
excerpt: There are two different kinds of "translation" in this product, handled two different ways. 1. UI chrome — admin/organizer panel and site labels Buttons, labels
text: There are two different kinds of "translation" in this product, handled two different ways. 1. UI chrome — admin/organizer panel and site labels Buttons, labels, error messages — the fixed text around the product, not content an organizer wrote. This is what Admin → Languages and Admin → Translations manage. Add a language Admin → Languages → Add: enter a code (e.g. fr), display name, native name, whether it's right-to-left, and whether it's active. English is seeded by default and can't be deactivated or deleted. Only one language can be the default at a time — setting a new default reassigns it and activates that language automatically. Translate it Admin → Translations → pick the language → you'll see every UI string in the product next to its English default, with an editable box. Save a value to override it for that language; clear it back to empty to fall back to the English default again — there's no "half-translated" broken state, every untranslated string just shows English until you fill it in. Export / import Translations can be exported as JSON (the full effective set — your overrides plus English defaults for anything untranslated) and re-imported, so translation work can be done offline or handed to a translator and brought back in. Import validates every key against the known key catalog and ignores anything it doesn't recognize, so a malformed file can't corrupt the table. 2. Event/organizer content — per-locale fields on the content itself Event titles and descriptions, FAQ answers, category names, and organizer bios are translated separately, directly on each model, editable per-locale right in that item's own editor (the event editor, the category editor, etc.) — not through the Translations screen. If you haven't entered a translation for a given locale, that content falls back to whichever locale it does have. Mobile apps use bundled translations, not live ones The customer and scanner apps ship their own translation files built into the app — they don't fetch UI strings from the server at runtime. Changing a translation in Admin → Translations affects the website and panels immediately; it does not affect the mobile apps until their own translation files are updated and the app is rebuilt.

title: Backups
excerpt: No built-in backup/restore feature As of this release, PerfectEvents does not include an in-app backup or restore tool. Set up backups at the server/hosting lev
text: No built-in backup/restore feature As of this release, PerfectEvents does not include an in-app backup or restore tool. Set up backups at the server/hosting level, the same way you would for any web application. What to back up The database — every order, ticket, event, and account record lives here. This is the part that matters most. storage/app/public (or your S3 bucket, if you're using S3 storage) — uploaded media: event covers, organizer logos, branding assets. .env — your app key and credentials. Losing this without a copy means losing the ability to decrypt anything the app encrypted (encrypted session/cookie data). How to actually do it cPanel / shared hosting — most hosts offer a "Backup" or "JetBackup" tool that handles both the database and files on a schedule; use it, or set up a cron-triggered mysqldump to a location outside your web root (and ideally off-server — an S3 bucket, or your host's remote backup destination). VPS — a scheduled mysqldump plus a file sync (rsync/restic/etc.) of storage/app/public to off-server storage. Any standard Linux backup tool works; there's nothing PerfectEvents-specific about the backup itself. Managed database (RDS, PlanetScale, etc.) — use the provider's built-in automated snapshots. Restoring Restore the database dump and the media files, and make sure storage/app/installed.json (the install lock — see Troubleshooting the installer) comes back too if your backup didn't already include the whole storage/ directory — a restore that only covers the database can otherwise leave the app thinking it isn't installed.

title: Multi-Country & Multi-Currency
excerpt: Everything money-related in this product is driven from two small reference tables — Admin → Currencies and Admin → Countries — plus the country-and-currency-sp
text: Everything money-related in this product is driven from two small reference tables — Admin → Currencies and Admin → Countries — plus the country-and-currency-specific overrides layered on top of them. A fresh install ships with just USD active and no country-specific overrides, and behaves exactly like a single-currency platform until you configure more. Nothing below is required reading for a single-country, single-currency install. Currencies Admin → Currencies is the source of truth for how money renders everywhere — symbol, decimal places, thousands/decimal separators, and whether the symbol sits to the left or right of the amount. Every platform (web, PDFs, emails, both Flutter apps) formats a given amount identically because they all read from this same table via /api/v1/config. Activate as many currencies as you like; organizers price each event's ticket types in whichever active currency they choose, and every ticket type on one event must share the same currency — checkout rejects a basket that somehow mixed them. Countries Admin → Countries is a reference list (code, name, dial code) used by venue address forms, the buyer phone-number picker, and event discovery's country filter. It's pure reference data — adding a country here doesn't change any pricing or tax behavior by itself. Tax Rates Admin → Tax Rates lets you set a tax rate (VAT, GST, sales tax — whatever you label it), inclusive or exclusive, per country. At checkout, the applicable rate is looked up by the event's venue country — not the buyer's billing address, since this product doesn't collect one. An event with no venue, or a venue in a country with no configured rate, falls back to the single global rate in Admin → Settings → General. Whatever rate actually applied is stamped onto the order at checkout time, so changing a country's rate later never rewrites a past order's receipt. Place-of-supply tax only This resolves tax by where the event happens, which covers the common case (a ticketed event has a physical or nominal venue location). Buyer-location-based tax rules (e.g. some digital-services VAT regimes) aren't modeled — there's no buyer billing address anywhere in this product to base that on. Currency Fees Admin → Currency Fees overrides the platform service fee (percentage + fixed amount, normally set in Settings → General) for one specific currency. You'll usually only need the fixed-amount half: a flat "50" fixed fee is 50 cents in USD but a very different real amount in a currency with different decimal places (0 for JPY, 3 for BHD/KWD/OMR). Leave either number blank to keep using the general value for just that half. Organizer defaults An organizer's Profile page has an optional home country and default currency. Neither is required, and neither restricts what an organizer can actually do — they're pre-fills only: a new event's currency dropdown defaults to the organizer's own default currency instead of the platform default, once set. Payment gateway compatibility Each payment gateway declares which currencies it can actually settle — Stripe and PayPal accept any; Razorpay is INR-only; Paystack covers NGN/GHS/ZAR/KES/USD. Checkout only ever offers a gateway that supports the order's currency, and the payment layer itself rejects a mismatched attempt even if bypassed at the UI level — this can't be worked around by editing a Blade view or the Flutter app, since the compatibility list lives on the gateway class itself, not the presentation layer. Discovery & coupons Buyers can filter events by country in the public site and the customer app, alongside the existing city filter. Coupons follow one rule: a percentage coupon works across any currency; a fixed-amount coupon is scoped to one currency (chosen when you create it) and simply won't apply to an order in a different one. Payouts stay manual regardless None of the above changes how payouts work — see Payouts. An organizer running events in more than one currency simply accumulates a sepa

title: Modules
excerpt: Some features ship as self-contained modules inside script/modules/. They're listed under Admin → System → Modules. ModuleWhat it doesSettings PaymentsThe payme
text: Some features ship as self-contained modules inside script/modules/. They're listed under Admin → System → Modules. ModuleWhat it doesSettings PaymentsThe payment gateways used at checkout and for refunds.Admin → Settings → Payment gateways. See Integrations. SMSText-message delivery for notifications.Admin → Settings → SMS. See SMS. Software UpdateChecks and installs the signed update package that comes with each release.Admin → System → Updates. See Updating the product. Built-in modules are always on All three are part of the product: they can't be disabled or removed, they need no licence key of their own, and they're updated together with everything else by the normal update package. You never download or update a module separately. Add-on modules The Modules page can also enable, disable and remove add-on modules. When you remove one you choose whether to keep its data: tick "Also delete its database tables" only if you're sure — that rolls back the module's migrations and its data is gone for good.

title: Maps & Venue Locations
excerpt: The customer app shows events on a map (Discover → the map button) and a venue map with a Directions button on each event page. Both use the venue's map locatio
text: The customer app shows events on a map (Discover → the map button) and a venue map with a Directions button on each event page. Both use the venue's map location. Give a venue its location On Admin → Venues (or the venue section of an organizer's event editor), fill in Map location. Paste either: the coordinates — in Google Maps, right-click the place and click the numbers at the top of the menu to copy them (e.g. 51.5072, -0.1276), or a Google Maps or OpenStreetMap link to the place. Leave it blank to keep a venue off the map; its events still show everywhere else. Online events never appear on the map. Map provider Admin → Settings → App → Maps sets what the app's maps draw. FieldWhat to enter Map providerOpenStreetMap / tile provider (the default) or Google Maps. Switching takes effect on the app's next launch. Tile URLA raster tile URL template with {z}, {x} and {y} placeholders, including your API key. Blank = OpenStreetMap's public tiles. AttributionThe credit line your tile provider requires — required whenever you set a Tile URL. The map adds the © sign itself. Use a tile provider for a live app OpenStreetMap's public tiles are fine while you test, but their usage policy doesn't allow heavy traffic from apps. Before launch, create a free or paid account with a provider such as MapTiler, Stadia Maps or Thunderforest, and paste their raster tile URL and attribution here. Changes reach the app on its next launch — no rebuild. The app identifies itself to tile servers with its app ID (the APP_ID in your config file), as tile providers' policies ask. Google Maps Google Maps needs your own API key built into the customer app: In the Google Cloud console, enable Maps SDK for Android and Maps SDK for iOS, and create an API key. Restrict it to those two APIs and to your app's package name / bundle ID. Add it to the customer app's config file as "GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY": "your-key", then rebuild the app. Android and iOS both read it from there. Choose Google Maps under Admin → Settings → App → Maps. An app built without a key keeps drawing the tile map, even with Google Maps selected, so switching the setting never leaves anyone with a blank map. Google Maps draws its own credit line; the Tile URL and Attribution fields only apply to the tile map.

title: Door Check-in & Offline Use
excerpt: Setting up door staff An organizer creates scanner accounts under Organizer → Door staff and ticks the venues each person works. Staff can scan every one of tha
text: Setting up door staff An organizer creates scanner accounts under Organizer → Door staff and ticks the venues each person works. Staff can scan every one of that organizer's events at those venues, including events added later. "Revoke access" removes every venue and signs the person out of the Scanner app straight away. Scanning Staff sign in to the Scanner app, pick the event, and point the camera at the ticket's QR code. Each scan answers Admitted, Already used (with when) or a reason the ticket isn't valid. The event screen shows live door numbers — checked in vs. expected — refreshed every 20 seconds. Find a guest For a guest whose phone died or who can't find their ticket, tap Find a guest on the event screen and type at least two characters of their name, email or ticket code. Each result shows whether that ticket is already in, and a Check in button. When the connection drops A scan the server doesn't answer — no signal, or the server is briefly unavailable — is saved on the phone and shown as "Saved". The Scanner app keeps re-sending saved scans in the background until the server answers, so the queue at the door keeps moving. While a scan is saved, check that ticket by eye. A chip on the event screen shows how many scans are waiting; tap it to see them or Send now. If a saved scan later comes back as anything other than admitted (for example, the same ticket was already used at another entrance), it moves to Need a look so staff can find that guest and check their ticket. Saved scans survive the app being closed. Buyers' tickets offline The customer app keeps a copy of the buyer's tickets on their phone each time the wallet loads. With no connection, the wallet shows that copy with a notice of when it was saved — the QR codes still scan at the door. The copy is deleted when the buyer signs out.

title: Toolchain Setup
excerpt: The mobile apps are entirely optional — skip this whole section if you're only selling through the website. If you do want the apps, here's what to install firs
text: The mobile apps are entirely optional — skip this whole section if you're only selling through the website. If you do want the apps, here's what to install first. 1. Flutter, via FVM The project pins an exact Flutter version (currently 3.47.2) via FVM (Flutter Version Management), so your local Flutter matches what the app was built and tested against instead of whatever's globally installed. dart pub global activate fvm cd flutter/apps/customer # and again in flutter/apps/scanner fvm install # installs the pinned version from .fvmrc fvm use # points this project at it Run every Flutter/Dart command through fvm from here on — fvm flutter run, fvm dart run, etc. 2. Platform SDKs Android — Android Studio (or just the command-line SDK tools) with a recent Android SDK/NDK, on any OS. iOS — Xcode, which means a Mac. This is an Apple requirement, not this product's — there's no way to build or sign an iOS app without one. 3. Verify it worked Each app is a normal Flutter project. Open flutter/apps/customer (or apps/scanner) in Android Studio or VS Code, or from a terminal: cd flutter/apps/customer fvm flutter pub get fvm flutter analyze # should print "No issues found!"
