If that passes clean, you're set up correctly. See Project structure next for how the pieces fit together.

title: Project Structure
excerpt: flutter/ └─ apps/ ├─ customer/ ← discovery, checkout, ticket wallet, orders, profile (V1, in this release) │ ├─ lib/core/ ← API client, auth/token storage, desi
text: flutter/ └─ apps/ ├─ customer/ ← discovery, checkout, ticket wallet, orders, profile (V1, in this release) │ ├─ lib/core/ ← API client, auth/token storage, design tokens, shared UI, formatting │ ├─ lib/src/ ← the app's features │ ├─ assets/ ← fonts + default branding │ ├─ config/ ← dev.json (you create this), prod.json.example │ └─ tool/rebrand/ ← the rebranding kit — see Rebranding the apps └─ scanner/ ← staff auth, event select, QR scan + check-in, scan history (V1, in this release) └─ (same layout) Why two separate apps, not one Customers and door staff have different users, different permissions, different navigation, and different release cadences — a customer downloading your ticketing app has no reason to also download door-staff scanning tools. Each app is a complete, self-contained Flutter project with its own pubspec.yaml, android/, ios/, store listing, icon and config. Building or shipping one never touches the other. Opening an app Open flutter/apps/customer (or flutter/apps/scanner) in Android Studio or VS Code, then run flutter pub get. No monorepo tool, no shared package to set up. Both apps contain the same lib/core/ code; if you change something there and want it in both apps, make the change in each. Per-app commands Run these from inside the app's directory (e.g. flutter/apps/customer): fvm flutter run --dart-define-from-file=config/dev.json fvm flutter build appbundle --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json # Android fvm flutter build ipa --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json # iOS, Mac required See Building Android and Building iOS for the full release process.

title: Config Files
excerpt: Each app is pointed at your backend via a small JSON file passed at build/run time with --dart-define-from-file — not a .env file bundled into the app (which wo
text: Each app is pointed at your backend via a small JSON file passed at build/run time with --dart-define-from-file — not a .env file bundled into the app (which would ship its contents inside the compiled binary, readable by anyone). config/prod.json.example Each app has its own config/ folder (flutter/apps/customer/config and flutter/apps/scanner/config), so the two apps can point at different values. { "API_BASE_URL": "https://your-domain.com/api/v1", "ENV": "prod", "APP_NAME": "Your App Name", "APP_ID": "com.yourcompany.events", "GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY": "" } Copy this to prod.json and fill in: KeyValue API_BASE_URLYour installed backend's /api/v1 URL. Required. ENVprod for store builds. APP_NAMEThe same name as Admin → Settings → Branding → App name. Only shown on a very first launch with no internet; after that the app uses the name from your settings. APP_IDThe app's package name / bundle ID (the package_id from rebranding). Sent to map tile servers, whose usage policies ask apps to identify themselves. GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEYCustomer app, optional: your Google Maps key, needed only if you choose Google Maps in Admin → Settings → App → Maps. Leave it blank to use tile maps. This key ends up in the app, like every mobile maps key, so restrict it to your app in the Google Cloud console. See Maps & venue locations. prod.json isn't committed (it's your real endpoint), only the .example is. config/dev.json Same shape, for local development against a dev/staging backend — create this yourself, typically pointing at http://localhost:8000/api/v1 or a staging URL. Not committed either. Everything else comes from the API, not a config file Brand name, logo, colors, enabled languages/currencies/payment gateways — the app fetches all of that from GET /api/v1/config on launch (cached locally, with a bundled fallback for offline first-launch). Changing your brand color in Admin → Settings takes effect in the app the next time it launches, no rebuild required. See Admin-configurable vs. rebuild for exactly where the line is.

title: Rebranding the Apps
excerpt: Most of an app's brand — its in-app name, logo, colors, support email — is already Admin-configurable at runtime, no rebuild needed (see Admin-configurable vs.
text: Most of an app's brand — its in-app name, logo, colors, support email — is already Admin-configurable at runtime, no rebuild needed (see Admin-configurable vs. rebuild). The rebrand kit exists for the handful of things a store listing and the OS itself need baked into the compiled app: launcher icon, splash screen, the name shown under the icon, and the Android/iOS package id. Run it once per app before you build for release. 1. Prepare your assets A 1024×1024 PNG icon (no transparency for iOS), and optionally a splash logo image. 2. Copy the example config Each app carries its own copy of the kit. Run these from inside the app's folder: cd flutter/apps/customer cp tool/rebrand/customer.example.yaml tool/rebrand/customer.yaml cd ../scanner cp tool/rebrand/scanner.example.yaml tool/rebrand/scanner.yaml 3. Edit the config In tool/rebrand/customer.yaml (and separately for scanner.yaml), set the app name, package id, and the path to your icon (relative to the config file itself, or absolute). Each app needs its own values — a customer ticketing app and a staff scanning app shouldn't share one package id or store listing. 4. Run it cd flutter/apps/customer && dart run tool/rebrand.dart customer cd flutter/apps/scanner && dart run tool/rebrand.dart scanner Add --dry-run first to preview the plan without changing anything. Each step (icon, splash, rename) is independent and safe to re-run if one fails partway — just fix the reported error and run it again. Only apps/<app>/android and apps/<app>/ios are touched. Still manual after running this Firebase — replace google-services.json and GoogleService-Info.plist with your own project's files, per app. Push notifications silently stay off until you do. See Firebase & push. iOS signing — open apps/<app>/ios/Runner.xcworkspace in Xcode, pick your own team under Signing & Capabilities, confirm the bundle id matches your config. A Mac is required — there's no way around this for iOS. Store listings — changing the package id after you've already published creates a brand-new listing rather than renaming the existing one. Decide your final package id before your first submission. Native permission strings (e.g. the camera-usage description the scanner app shows) — edit Info.plist/AndroidManifest.xml directly if you want different wording; the defaults work for most buyers. Android's namespace (in build.gradle.kts, distinct from applicationId since AGP 8) is left as-is by the kit — edit it by hand too if you want it to match your new applicationId. A mismatch is valid and builds fine either way. Troubleshooting "Config file not found" You need to copy the .example.yaml to a plain .yaml first (step 2) — the example file itself is never read directly. "Icon file not found" / "Splash image not found" The path in your config is relative to the config file's own directory, not to flutter/.

title: Admin-Configurable vs. Rebuild
excerpt: Both apps fetch GET /api/v1/config on launch (cached, with a bundled fallback for offline first-launch), so a lot of "branding" is live and instant — change it
text: Both apps fetch GET /api/v1/config on launch (cached, with a bundled fallback for offline first-launch), so a lot of "branding" is live and instant — change it in Admin, and it's reflected the next time the app opens, no store update required. Admin → Settings → App: support contact and mobile app links. Admin — no rebuildRebuild — needs the kit and/or a new build App name shown inside the app, brand colors (light/dark), logo, support linksStore-listing display name, launcher/app icon, splash image + native splash color Enabled locales, translations, RTLBundled fonts Enabled payment gatewaysFirebase project (google-services.json / GoogleService-Info.plist) Feature flagsAPI base URL (baked in via --dart-define-from-file) Android/iOS package id, native permission strings, deep-link / associated domains, signing If you only need the left column You don't need the rebrand kit at all — just use Admin → Settings → Branding. The kit and a rebuild are only necessary if you're publishing your own store listing under your own identity (own icon, own package id) rather than using the apps as-shipped. See Rebranding the apps for how to actually change the right-hand column, and Admin vs. rebuild for the same split as it applies to the website/panels rather than the apps.

title: Building Android (AAB)
excerpt: Do this once you've rebranded the app and set your real production API URL. 1. Generate a signing key If you don't already have one for this app: keytool -genke
text: Do this once you've rebranded the app and set your real production API URL. 1. Generate a signing key If you don't already have one for this app: keytool -genkey -v -keystore upload-keystore.jks -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 -alias upload Store this file and its passwords somewhere safe and durable — losing it means you can never publish an update to an already-live app under the same listing again. Play App Signing (below) softens this for future re-key scenarios but the upload key itself still matters. 2. Point Gradle at it Create apps/<app>/android/key.properties (not committed) with your keystore path and passwords, and reference it from android/app/build.gradle.kts's signing config — standard Flutter/Android release signing, no product-specific step here. Flutter's own "Build and release an Android app" guide covers the exact Gradle wiring if you haven't set this up before. 3. Build cd apps/customer # or apps/scanner fvm flutter build appbundle --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json Output lands at build/app/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab. Build each app separately — they're independent binaries. 4. Play App Signing When you first upload to Play Console, opt into Play App Signing — Google re-signs your upload key with their own app-signing key for distribution, which means a lost/compromised upload key later is recoverable (you can request a reset) rather than catastrophic. Test the bundle before submitting Use Play Console's internal testing track first — install the actual AAB on a real device via Play's internal app sharing before pushing to production review.

title: Building iOS (IPA)
excerpt: Apple requires Xcode to build, sign, and submit an iOS app — there is no way to produce an installable/submittable IPA from Windows or Linux. If you don't have
text: Apple requires Xcode to build, sign, and submit an iOS app — there is no way to produce an installable/submittable IPA from Windows or Linux. If you don't have a Mac, this is the one part of publishing you'll need to borrow, rent (a cloud Mac service), or outsource for. 1. Apple Developer Program You need a paid Apple Developer account (individual or organization) before you can create the App ID, provisioning profiles, or submit to TestFlight/App Store. 2. Set up signing in Xcode Open apps/<app>/ios/Runner.xcworkspace (not the .xcodeproj) in Xcode. Under Signing & Capabilities, select your team and confirm the bundle identifier matches what you set during rebranding. "Automatically manage signing" is the simplest path for most buyers. 3. Build cd apps/customer # or apps/scanner fvm flutter build ipa --dart-define-from-file=config/prod.json Output lands under build/ios/ipa/. 4. Upload Use Xcode's Organizer (Window → Organizer, or drag the .ipa in via Transporter) to upload the build to App Store Connect, then attach it to a version in your app's listing there. TestFlight first Distribute to internal TestFlight testers before submitting for App Store review — it catches device-specific and provisioning problems earlier, and doesn't count against your review submissions.

title: Play Store Submission
excerpt: Submit the customer and scanner apps as separate listings — they're separate apps with separate audiences, not variants of one listing. Before you start A signe
text: Submit the customer and scanner apps as separate listings — they're separate apps with separate audiences, not variants of one listing. Before you start A signed AAB — see Building Android. App icon (512×512), feature graphic (1024×500), and at least 2 phone screenshots per app. A short description (80 chars) and full description (4000 chars). A privacy policy URL — required by Play regardless of what data you collect. A completed Data Safety form — declares what data the app collects/shares (account info, device identifiers for push notifications, payment info if the app handles it directly for a gateway). Content rating questionnaire, completed honestly for what the app actually does. Submission flow Create the app in Play Console, fill in the store listing (description, screenshots, icon, category — Events, most likely). Complete Data Safety and Content Rating. Upload your AAB to a testing track (internal → closed/open, optional) or straight to production. Submit for review. Review time Typically a few hours to a few days for a first submission; updates are usually faster. See Common rejections for what most often causes a bounce.

title: App Store Submission
excerpt: Same principle as Play: the customer and scanner apps are separate App Store listings. Before you start A build uploaded via Xcode/Transporter — see Building iO
text: Same principle as Play: the customer and scanner apps are separate App Store listings. Before you start A build uploaded via Xcode/Transporter — see Building iOS. App icon (1024×1024, no transparency), and screenshots for each required device size (at minimum the largest iPhone size Apple currently requires; App Store Connect will tell you exactly which sizes are missing). A privacy policy URL. App Privacy details (the "nutrition label") — what data is collected and whether it's linked to the user's identity or used for tracking. A demo account for reviewers, if login is required to see the app's core functionality — which it is here. Provide a working test account's credentials in the App Review notes so a reviewer can actually get past login. Submission flow Create the app in App Store Connect, fill in the listing (description, keywords, screenshots, category — Events or Lifestyle). Complete App Privacy. Attach your uploaded build to the version. Fill in App Review notes — demo credentials, and a one-paragraph explanation of what the app does if it isn't obvious from the listing alone. Submit for review. Review time Usually 24–48 hours, though it varies. See Common rejections — Apple's review is generally stricter than Play's, and the demo-account issue below is the single most common reason a ticketing/scanning app bounces on first submission.

title: Common Rejections
excerpt: "Reviewer can't get past login" (Apple, most common) Cause: The customer app requires an account, and no working demo credentials were provided. Fix: Create a r
text: "Reviewer can't get past login" (Apple, most common) Cause: The customer app requires an account, and no working demo credentials were provided. Fix: Create a real test account on your live/demo backend and put its email and password directly in the App Review notes field. If your backend requires email verification, either pre-verify the reviewer account or note in the review notes that it's already verified. "App is not functional" / "app is placeholder content" (Apple) Cause: A fresh install with no events yet, or a review account tied to an empty organizer, looks empty to a reviewer with nothing to click into. Fix: Make sure whatever backend your submitted build points at has real, published events with images before you submit — don't submit against a totally empty install. Missing or incomplete Data Safety / App Privacy declaration Cause: Both stores reject a listing whose privacy declaration doesn't match what the app actually does — for example, not declaring that push notification tokens or purchase data are collected. Fix: Be thorough and honest: account info, device/push tokens, and payment-related data (even if a payment SDK handles the sensitive part) should generally all be declared. Camera permission rejected (scanner app) Cause: The scanner app's camera-usage permission string is vague or missing context for why it needs the camera. Fix: Make sure the permission description clearly explains it's for scanning ticket QR codes at check-in — edit it directly in Info.plist/AndroidManifest.xml if the default wording needs to be more specific for your brand. Payment flow issues (Apple specifically) Cause: Apple requires In-App Purchase for digital goods/services consumed within the app, but physical/real-world event tickets are generally treated as a "reader"-style external service and allowed to use a regular payment gateway — reviewers occasionally flag this incorrectly regardless. Fix: If flagged, respond in Resolution Center explaining that tickets are for a real-world, in-person event (not digital content consumed in-app) — this is a well-established exception category, but worth stating plainly rather than assuming the reviewer already knows your app's specific case. Metadata rejection (both stores) Cause: Screenshots showing content that doesn't match the current build, or a description mentioning features not actually present. Fix: Keep screenshots and description in sync with what you actually ship — easy to let slip after rebranding if you reuse old screenshots.

title: Updating the Product
excerpt: Every release comes with a ready-made update package. You install it from the admin panel — no FTP, no SSH, no re-running the install wizard, and your data, upl
text: Every release comes with a ready-made update package. You install it from the admin panel — no FTP, no SSH, no re-running the install wizard, and your data, uploads and .env are never touched. 1. Find the package In the release download, open the Updates/ folder. It holds: FileWhat it's for perfect-events-vX-to-vY.zipThe server update. Installs over exactly version X and takes you to Y. Upload this one in Admin. perfect-events-mobile-vX-to-vY.zipOnly present when the apps changed: the changed flutter/ files plus a DELETED.txt. See Mobile apps below. Your installed version is shown at the top of Admin → System → Updates. If you're more than one release behind, install each package in turn (X→Y, then Y→Z); a package refuses to install over any version other than the one it was built from. 2. Read the changelog Check the changelog for every version you're crossing. Anything you have to do by hand — a new cron line, a raised PHP version, rebuilding the apps — is listed under that version's "Updating" note. 3. Back up Take a database dump and a copy of storage/app/public (skip that if your uploads live on S3). See Backups. The updater backs up and restores the files it replaces by itself, but database changes can't be rolled back — that's what your dump is for. The Updates page won't start until you tick "I have a current backup". 4. Install Go to Admin → System → Updates. Tick the backup confirmation, choose the perfect-events-vX-to-vY.zip file and click Install. Keep the page open while it runs. It works in three short steps, one request each, so it fits inside a shared host's time limits: Verifying — checks the package's signature, that it's newer than what you run and built from your version, that your server meets its requirements, that every file it will replace is writable, and that there's enough disk space. Applying — turns on maintenance mode, backs up every file it's about to change, then swaps in the new ones. Migrating — runs the database migrations, clears caches, records the new version and turns maintenance mode off. If the page stops moving (a closed tab, a timed-out request), just reload it: an interrupted run resumes, or is rolled back to the previous files if it can't continue. Only packages signed by the author install Each package is signed, and your copy checks the signature before it unpacks anything. A file that was altered, or didn't come from the official release, is rejected with "The package signature is missing or invalid". If an update is refused MessageWhat to do Version … is not newer than the installed …You've already installed it. Nothing to do. This incremental package applies to X, but Y is installedYou picked the wrong package. Use the one whose name starts with your installed version. Requirements not metThe release needs a newer PHP version or extension. Upgrade it in your hosting panel, then retry. These files were changed since the last update…You edited files the update also changes. Copy your edits somewhere safe, restore the originals, update, then re-apply them — see Preserving customizations. The web server can't write to…Fix the permissions on the listed files so the web server user owns them, then retry. Not enough free disk spaceThe updater needs room for the new files and a backup of the old ones. Free some space, then retry. The upload is rejected as too largePackages up to 12 MB upload from the page. If your PHP upload_max_filesize / post_max_size are lower, raise them to at least 16M. If a run fails after it started replacing files, every file is put back automatically and the page tells you so. In the rare case that restoring fails too, the site stays in maintenance mode and the message names the folder holding the backup — copy those files back over the install, then run php artisan up. Built-in modules Payments, SMS and Software Update are part of the product and update with it — they have no separate update or licence of their own. See Modules. Mobile apps The server update

title: Backup & Restore Around an Update
excerpt: This is the same process described in full on Backups — there's no in-app backup/restore tool at any point, including around an update. The only thing specific
text: This is the same process described in full on Backups — there's no in-app backup/restore tool at any point, including around an update. The only thing specific to an update is timing: take the backup immediately before you start, not "recently." Before updating Database dump. storage/app/public (or confirm your S3 bucket needs no action — it isn't touched by a code update either way). Your current .env and, if you've made any, your customized files. If an update goes wrong Restore the previous release's script/ code (keep it around until the update is confirmed working — don't delete the old version immediately). Restore the database dump you just took, not an older one — the goal is undoing the update, not losing work that happened since your last routine backup. Clear caches (php artisan config:clear etc., or Admin → System's button) and verify. Migrations can be one-way Some database migrations aren't cleanly reversible (a column drop, a data transformation). Restoring your pre-update database dump is the reliable rollback path — don't rely on php artisan migrate:rollback alone for an update you're trying to fully undo.

title: Preserving Customizations
excerpt: PerfectEvents doesn't have a formal plugin/hook/override-file system. If you edit application code directly, an update that touches the same file will overwrite
text: PerfectEvents doesn't have a formal plugin/hook/override-file system. If you edit application code directly, an update that touches the same file will overwrite your change — there's no automatic merge. This page is about minimizing that pain, not eliminating it entirely. The practical strategy: version control Put your install under git from day one (a private repo, not the CodeCanyon zip's own history). Commit before every update. When a new release lands: Commit or stash your current state. Apply the new release's files as a new commit (or a merge, if you're comfortable with git — this is exactly what a merge is good at: reconciling your changes against upstream changes to the same files). Resolve any conflicts — git will tell you exactly which files both you and the update touched, rather than silently discarding either side. This turns "did I lose my customization?" from a manual diff-everything exercise into git doing what it's built for. Prefer settings and content over code, where you can Anything already covered by Admin vs. rebuild — branding, CMS pages, notification copy, homepage layout, translations — survives every update automatically, because it lives in the database, not in a file an update replaces. Before editing code for something, check the settings reference — it may already be a setting. Where the codebase is actually built to be extended A few areas use a driver/registry pattern specifically so a genuinely new capability doesn't require touching existing files, which makes it much easier to carry forward across updates: Payment gateways — adding a new one is one new class implementing PaymentGateway plus one config entry; CheckoutService and the rest of checkout never need to change. Homepage sections — new section types are registered the same way, by key, rather than hardcoded into the homepage view. A new file you add yourself (a new gateway class, for example) is untouched by an update almost by definition — it's changes to shipped files that are at risk. Be extra careful editing shipped files that carry business logic A styling tweak to a Blade view is low-risk to redo after an update. A change inside CheckoutService, a payment gateway driver, or anything money/ticket/auth-related is higher-stakes to lose track of — this is exactly the kind of change version control is worth having before you make it.

title: API Overview
excerpt: Everything under /api/v1 is the same API the Flutter apps use — there's no separate "public API" with reduced functionality. A token-holding client can do anyth
text: Everything under /api/v1 is the same API the Flutter apps use — there's no separate "public API" with reduced functionality. A token-holding client can do anything the account type it belongs to is allowed to do. Authentication Token-based via Laravel Sanctum. Two ways to get a token: RouteNotes POST /api/v1/auth/loginEmail + password + a required device_name. Returns a bearer token. POST /api/v1/auth/registerSelf-registration — customer accounts only. Organizers apply through the website; staff accounts are created by their organizer. Both are rate-limited against brute force. Send the token on every subsequent request: Authorization: Bearer {token} Tokens don't auto-expire. POST /api/v1/auth/logout revokes just the current token (other devices/sessions stay logged in). Abilities — what a token can do Coarse, per account type, checked at the middleware layer (not just in application logic — a staff token literally cannot reach a route outside its ability): Account typeAbilities Admin* — everything Organizer* — everything (scoped to their own data by policy checks, not by ability) Stafftickets.scan only Customertickets.view only This is a separate, coarser mechanism from the roles/permissions system described in the permissions matrix — abilities gate which API routes a token can reach at all; roles/permissions further gate what an authenticated user can do once there. Key route groups GroupNotes Discovery — events, categories, pages, organizersFully public, no auth, IP rate-limited. CheckoutAuth required — no guest checkout, by design. Scanner (/api/v1/scanner/*)Requires the tickets.scan ability — a staff token can reach these and nothing outside them. Payment webhooks (/api/v1/webhooks/{gateway})Public/unauthenticated — trust comes from each gateway's own signature verification, not a token. Profile, tickets, orders, notificationsThe authenticated user's own data. Response shape Successful responses wrap their payload in a consistent envelope ({"data": ...}); paginated list endpoints include a meta.pagination block. Errors return a consistent shape with an HTTP status and a machine-readable error code (for example EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED when checkout is blocked pending email verification) rather than just a human-readable message. What's deliberately not here yet No refresh-token rotation, no 2FA-over-API challenge, and abilities don't go any finer-grained than the four rows above. These are known, deferred scope — not gaps to work around.

title: Permissions Matrix
excerpt: Roles are fixed in this version — admin, organizer, staff. Customers don't get a role at all; plain account type is enough for what a customer can do. Creating
text: Roles are fixed in this version — admin, organizer, staff. Customers don't get a role at all; plain account type is enough for what a customer can do. Creating your own custom roles isn't available yet. What admin can toggle Admin → Roles & permissions lets you adjust which permissions organizer and staff are granted, from this fixed set of seven: PermissionDefault grantsToggleable in Admin? events.manage.ownorganizerYes orders.view.ownorganizerYes tickets.scanorganizer, staffYes staff.manageorganizerYes events.approveadmin only (structural)No — admin-only by design settings.manageadmin only (structural)No — admin-only by design payouts.approveadmin only (structural)No — admin-only by design The admin account type bypasses permission checks entirely rather than being granted these as stored rows — "admin can do everything" is structural, not a setting you could accidentally turn off. Edits you make here are preserved across updates/reseeds — the underlying seeder only applies its defaults the first time a role has zero permissions, so re-running it never clobbers a change you've made. How this differs from API token abilities Roles/permissions govern what an authenticated user can do inside the panels and API. Sanctum API tokens carry a separate, coarser ability (admin/ organizer → everything, staff → scanning only, customer → viewing their own tickets) checked at the route-middleware level before a permission check is even reached — see the API overview.

title: Troubleshooting Index
excerpt: If you're stuck, check these first Requirements/Permissions step won't turn green — a missing PHP extension or wrong file permissions. "Test connection" fails o
text: If you're stuck, check these first Requirements/Permissions step won't turn green — a missing PHP extension or wrong file permissions. "Test connection" fails on the Database step — wrong host or a cPanel account-prefix mismatch. A published event isn't showing on the public site — usually still awaiting approval, or the organizer account itself isn't approved. A payment succeeded at the gateway but the order stays "pending" — almost always the webhook URL. Emails aren't sending — port/encryption mismatch, or still on the log driver. Admin → System shows a stale cron heartbeat — the cron entry isn't actually firing. Ticket PDFs/emails never arrive even though the order is paid — the queue isn't draining. Mobile push notifications never arrive — Firebase config mismatch, most often a wrong package/bundle id. A coupon code doesn't discount the order — it fails silently by design; check its eligibility rules. The site redirects back to the install wizard after already being installed — the install lock file went missing, usually from an incomplete restore/redeploy. A published event isn't showing on the public site Cause: Either the event itself is still Pending (awaiting admin approval) rather than Published, or its organizer account isn't Approved yet — an unapproved organizer can't have anything go public no matter what the event's own status is. Fix: Check both independently in Admin — see Approvals. A payment succeeded at the gateway but the order stays "pending" Cause: Orders only move to paid when the gateway's webhook fires and verifies — the browser redirect back to your site after payment is a UX convenience, not what confirms payment. If the webhook URL isn't registered correctly, or its secret doesn't match, the webhook is rejected and the order never updates even though the buyer was actually charged. Fix: Re-check the exact webhook URL and secret for that gateway against its integration page, and check the gateway's own dashboard for failed webhook delivery attempts (most providers log these with the exact rejection reason). Admin → System shows a stale cron heartbeat Cause: Your cron entry either isn't installed, points at the wrong PHP binary, or uses a relative/wrong path to artisan. Fix: See Cron & queue workers — confirm the exact command with your host, including which PHP binary resolves to 8.3+ on their cron environment specifically (it's sometimes different from your shell's default php). Ticket PDFs/emails never arrive even though the order is paid Cause: Almost always the same root cause as above — if cron isn't running, the scheduled queue drain isn't running either, so queued jobs (PDF generation, email, push) pile up and never execute. Fix: Fix the cron heartbeat first; queued jobs will drain on the next tick once it is. Admin → System also shows pending/failed job counts if you want to confirm the backlog directly. Mobile push notifications never arrive Cause: Most commonly a Firebase project mismatch — the app's bundled google-services.json/GoogleService-Info.plist doesn't match the project your server's FCM_CREDENTIALS service account belongs to, or the push channel is still off in settings. Fix: See Firebase & push — double check the package/bundle id matches between the Flutter app and the Firebase project exactly. A coupon code doesn't discount the order Cause: This is by design, not a bug — an ineligible coupon (expired, not yet started, over its redemption limit, or below the minimum order amount) silently lets checkout proceed at full price rather than blocking the order. Fix: Check the coupon's own rules in Admin/Organizer → Coupons — see Coupons. Still stuck? Check the FAQ, or your CodeCanyon listing's support policy for how to reach the developer directly.

title: FAQ
excerpt: Do I need the mobile apps to sell tickets? No. The website — public storefront, checkout, Admin, Organizer panel — is fully functional on its own. The Flutter a
text: Do I need the mobile apps to sell tickets? No. The website — public storefront, checkout, Admin, Organizer panel — is fully functional on its own. The Flutter apps are an optional add-on for buyers who want a native customer app and/or a door-staff scanner app in the app stores. Do I need Composer, Node, or SSH access to install this? No. The zip ships with vendor/ and built front-end assets already in place — upload, point your domain at script/public, and run the install wizard through a browser. See What's in the box. Can I use MariaDB instead of MySQL? No — MySQL 8.0+ specifically. The schema relies on MySQL 8–specific JSON functions and generated columns that MariaDB doesn't implement the same way. Which payment gateways are supported? Stripe, PayPal, Razorpay, and Paystack, out of the box — enable as many as you want simultaneously. See Integrations for each one's setup. Can I add a payment gateway that isn't in the list? Yes, if you (or a developer you hire) can write a Laravel class — the payment layer is a driver/contract pattern specifically so a new gateway doesn't require touching checkout logic. This is a code change, not something a non-developer can do purely from Admin. Is there a commission/fee system built in? Yes — a platform commission percentage (default or per-organizer override) is deducted at payout time. There's no automated money movement, though — payouts are a request/tracking workflow, and you actually pay organizers outside the platform. See Payouts. Can organizers have custom roles/permissions? Not in this version — roles are fixed (admin, organizer, staff), though you can adjust which permissions organizer/staff are granted. Custom roles are a planned future feature. See the permissions matrix. Does it support multiple languages? Yes — add languages and translate the UI from Admin, and event/organizer content is per-locale on the content itself. See Localization. Does it support guest checkout? No, deliberately — an account is required before purchase. This is a locked product decision, not a missing feature. Can a buyer get a partial refund for just some tickets in an order? Not yet — refunds are whole-order only in this version. See Refunds. Is there a built-in backup feature? No — see Backups for how to back up at the hosting/database level instead. How do I get support? Check your CodeCanyon item listing's support policy for how to reach the developer, and the troubleshooting index first for anything covered here.
